ABSTRACT
Carbon materials have the advantages of large surface area, high conductivity and stable chemical properties, 
and are widely used in the field of electrochemical energy storage. However, carbon materials currently have 
some problems such as high cost, complicated process and poor electrochemical performance. The development 
of low cost, environmental friendly and high specific capacitance porous carbon materials is of great significance 
for large-scale production and application. In addition, renewable, low-cost biomass materials are ideal pre -
cursors for the preparation of porous carbon materials. In this work, porous carbon materials were synthesized 
using ginkgo leaves as carbon source and KHCO
3 
as activator. The effect of activator mass on the structure and 
composition of porous carbon was studied in detail. The results show that when 3 g activator is added, the 
prepared carbon material (GCK-3) has a specific surface area of up to 2640 m
2 
g
� 1 
and a rich hierarchical pore 
structure (including micro, medium and large pores). In addition, the carbon material retains a certain amount of 
the heteroatoms of the biomass itself, which can generate additional pseudocapacitance. Due to the advantages 
of composition and structure, GCK-3 shows good electrochemical performance and rate performance. A sym -
metric supercapacitor assembled from two identical GCK-3 electrodes has an energy density of 13.7 Wh kg
� 1 
and 
exhibits good cycle stability with a capacitor retention rate of 100 % after 10,000 cycles. The green and low-cost 
carbon source precursor, simple synthesis method and excellent electrochemical properties all indicate that 
ginkgo leaf derived carbon materials have great application prospects.
1. Introduction
With the increasingly prominent resource and environmental prob -
lems, the development and demand of electronic equipment and new 
energy vehicles are increasing rapidly, and the development of low-cost 
and high-performance energy storage equipment has become particu -
larly important [ 1 , 2 ]. Supercapacitors have the characteristics of high 
power density, high coulomb efficiency and long cycle life, which are 
the energy storage devices concerned by many researchers [ 3 – 5 ]. 
Electrode materials play an important role in the electrochemical per -
formance of supercapacitors, and also involve the manufacturing cost of 
supercapacitors [ 6 ]. Therefore, the development of low-cost and 
high-performance electrode materials has become one of the main 
research goals of supercapacitors as energy storage devices.
Porous carbon materials have high surface area, high porosity, 
excellent electrical conductivity and chemical stability, and can be used 
as high-performance electrode materials for supercapacitors. At present, 
porous carbon materials mainly composed of micropores and small 
mesoporous are widely used as electrode materials [ 7 , 8 ]. However, 
porous carbon materials often have poor pore structure and closed 
pores, which is not conducive to the improvement of electrochemical 
properties [ 9 , 10 ]. To solve this problem, the pore size distribution of

carbon materials can be adjusted by chemical activation in the process of 
preparing porous carbon, which can convert the precursor into porous 
carbon by redox. The commonly used activator is KOH [ 11 – 13 ]. How -
ever, it is highly corrosive and easy to form K
2
CO
3 
with carbon mate -
rials, resulting in lower yield [ 14 ]. Relatively speaking, KHCO
3 
is less 
corrosive, low cost, and the melting point is also low, and it can also 
regulate the pore distribution of carbon materials through redox reac -
tion. At present, the preparation of carbon materials using KHCO
3 
as an 
activator has been reported. For example, Li et al. prepared 
iron-modified porous carbon with carbon spheres/nanoplate structure, 
but the preparation process is complicated and is not conducive to 
large-scale production [ 15 ]. Manyala et al. prepared porous carbon 
composed of micropores and mesoporous, but the electrochemical per -
formance was poor [ 16 ]. Feng et al. prepared hierarchical porous car -
bon, but the preparation process is complicated and the reaction 
conditions are harsh [ 17 ].
As a carbon precursor, biomass has the advantages of low cost, no 
pollution, rich resources, etc., and has been widely used in various fields 
(such as adsorption of contaminated water, electrochemical sensors, 
energy storage, supercapacitors, etc.) [ 18 – 20 ]. Among them, ginkgo 
leaves are mainly composed of cellulose, protein, carbohydrates and a 
small amount of inorganic minerals. These substances can provide het -
eroatomic (such as N, S, O) self-doping for carbon materials, which can 
affect the charge distribution of the carbon material, thus forming active 
regions on the surface of the carbon material [ 21 ]. In addition, ginkgo 
leaves have a special structure, and the porous skeleton of its derived 
carbon material can be considered to be composed of carbon nanosheets 
[ 22 ]. Therefore, carbon materials derived from ginkgo leaves should 
have broad application prospects in the field of supercapacitors.
As mentioned above, the mass production and application of porous 
carbon materials are limited due to its complex process, harsh reaction 
conditions and poor electrochemical properties. In order to solve these 
problems, we have chosen a low-cost, renewable ginkgo leaves as a 
precursor and a simple preparation method to synthesize porous carbon 
materials for supercapacitors. The structure-activity relationship be -
tween the structure composition and electrochemical properties of 
porous carbon materials was revealed by exploring the effects of pore 
structure, specific surface area and heteroatoms on electrochemical 
properties. This work has important theoretical significance and prac -
tical application value for the preparation of low cost and high perfor -
mance porous carbon.
2. Experimental
2.1. Synthesis of electrode materials
The purity of the chemical reagents in this experiment was analytical 
grade. Ginkgo leaves come from the same tree in Shanxi Normal Uni -
versity, and the leaves are in the same batch to ensure the consistency of 
the material, so the experimental data obtained have good compara -
bility. The preparation process of porous carbon materials is shown in 
Fig. 1 . First, the ginkgo leaves are washed with deionized water and 
dried. The ginkgo leaves are ground into powder through a grinder and 
passed through a 200-mesh sieve. The sifted 2 g powder was put into a 
nitrogen-protected tube furnace and carbonized at 750 
◦
C for 3 h. The 
heating rate is 5 
◦
C min
� 1
. The obtained product was stirred in 100 mL 2 
M HCl solution for 12 h, and then washed with deionized water several 
times until the pH of the supernatant was neutral. The final product is 
dried at 60 
◦
C, and the resulting carbon material is labeled GC. For 
comparison, 2, 3 and 4 g KHCO
3 
were added to 2 g ginkgo leaf powder, 
respectively. After mixing evenly, it is carbonized in a tube furnace. 
Other experimental conditions remained unchanged, and the obtained 
products were labeled as GCK-2, GCK-3 and GCK-4, respectively.
Structure characterization and electrochemical testing were written 
down in Supporting Information.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Structure and morphology
X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of ginkgo leaf derived carbon ma -
terials are shown in Fig. 2 a. All samples show a wide peak at 2 θ = 26
◦
and a weak peak at 2 θ = 44
◦
, corresponding to the (002) and (101) 
crystal faces of the graphite structure (JCPDS No. 41 – 1487), respec -
tively. The diffraction peak at 2 θ = 26
◦
is wider, indicating that the 
prepared carbon material mainly contains a large amount of amorphous 
carbon. The diffraction peak of the carbon material at 2 θ = 7
◦
represents 
the ordered structure of the graphene layer [ 23 ]. Among them, GC and 
GCK-3 have weak diffraction peaks at 2 θ = 7
◦
, and GCK-2 and GCK-4 
have strong diffraction peaks at 2 θ = 7
◦
, indicating that the ordering 
of the graphene layer in GC and GCK-3 is lower than that in GGK-2 and 
GCK-4.
Fig. 2 b shows the Raman spectrum of carbon materials. The D band is 
the characteristic peak of amorphous carbon, and the G band can indi -
cate the distribution degree of sp2 hybrid carbon atoms in carbon ma -
terials, and the intensity ratio (ID/IG) is usually used to measure the 
disorder degree of carbon materials [ 24 ]. In general, a larger ID/IG 
value indicates that the sample has more defects; a smaller ID/IG value 
indicates that the electrons in the sample are easily transported [ 25 ]. 
The figure shows that the ID/IG values of KHCO
3
-activated samples are 
all lower than GC, indicating that electrons are more easily transported 
in KHCO
3
-activated samples. Table S1 shows the Raman shifts in the 
D-band and G-band in different samples (Supporting Information). 
Among them, GCK-3 has the largest blue shift, indicating that it has the 
largest defect density, which is conducive to increasing the electro -
chemical active site [ 26 ]. In addition, the Raman peaks of GC and GCK-3 
are very sharp, indicating the presence of multilayer graphene in the 
sample, which is consistent with the XRD test results [ 27 – 31 ].
Fig. 2 c shows fourier transform infrared spectrophotometer (FTIR) 
analysis of ginkgo leaves and carbon materials. The figure shows that 
ginkgo leaves have a large number of functional groups, for example, the 
peaks at 1318, 1620, 1737 and 2925 cm
� 1 
correspond to C-H, C = C, C = O 
and methyl or methylidene, respectively. The wide peaks at 1070 and 
3426 cm
� 1 
represent the presence of a large number of OH [ 32 ].

Compared with ginkgo leaves, the OH peak intensity of carbon material 
was significantly weakened, indicating that a large amount of OH was 
removed during carbonization. At the same time, after carbonization of 
ginkgo leaves, the intensity of most characteristic peaks is obviously 
weakened or even disappeared, indicating that carbonization destroys 
most of the functional groups. The loss of functional groups means that 
ginkgo leaves are gradually converted to carbon material.
The surface element composition and functional group types of 
carbon materials were further studied using X-ray photoelectron spec -
troscopy (XPS). It can be seen from Fig. 2 d that carbon materials mainly 
contain C, N and O elements. Fig. 2 e shows the C1s high-resolution 
spectrum of the carbon materials. The C1s of GCK-3 can be divided 
into four peaks: C = C/C-C (284.6 eV), C-O (285.1 eV), C = O (286.4 eV) 
and O-C = O (290.1 eV) [ 33 , 34 ]. The C1s spectra of GC, GCK-2 and 
GCK-4 are consistent with that of GCK-3, indicating that the activation of 
KHCO
3 
does not change the electronic structure of C atoms, revealing 
that carbon materials have good stability. Fig. 2 f shows that the O1s of 
GCK-3 can be divided into three main peaks: C = O (531.9 eV), C-O 
(533.3 eV) and O = C-O (536.4 eV) [ 35 ], indicating that GCK-3 contains a 
large number of oxygen-containing functional groups, which is consis -
tent with the FTIR test results in Fig. 2 c. A large number of 
oxygen-containing functional groups can improve the hydrophilicity of 
carbon materials and provide additional pseudocapacitance. In addition, 
with the increase of KHCO
3
, the O1s spectra showed regular change 
(Supporting Information, Fig. S1 ). With the increase of the amount of 
KHCO
3
, the content of O = C-O gradually decreases, which is of great 
significance for regulating the surface active site of carbon materials. 
The high-resolution spectra of C1s and O1s are very smooth, and the 
peaks of the N1s spectrum are very bumpy, indicating that the signal of 
the N atom is weak, meaning that the content is very low (Supporting 
Information, Fig. S2 ). Since XPS can only analyze the surface of the 
sample, in order to obtain the exact amount of each element in the 
sample, we performed an elemental analyzer test. Table 1 shows the test 
results of the elemental analyzer, and the detected N, O and S atoms are 
all from the biomass itself. However, XPS did not detect the presence of S 
atoms, due to the different testing principles of XPS and the element 
analyzer. The content of O and N atoms in KHCO
3
-activated samples is 
lower than that of GC, indicating that CO
2 
released by KHCO
3 
can 
promote the volatilization of O and N atoms. In addition, GCK-3 has a 
high content of S atoms, indicating that an moderate amount of KHCO
3 
can effectively inhibit the volatilization of S atoms. The regulating effect

4. Conclusions
In summary, porous carbon materials derived from ginkgo leaves 
were successfully prepared by using ginkgo leaves as carbon source and 
KHCO
3 
as chemical activator. Because KHCO
3 
has an etching effect on 
carbon materials, the amount of KHCO
3 
has a significant impact on the 
morphology and structure of carbon materials. The experimental results 
show that when 3 g KHCO
3 
is added, the prepared GCK-3 has the largest 
specific surface area, good pore distribution, and the surface has a large 
number of oxygen-containing functional groups. The electrochemical 
test shows that in the electrolyte of 6 M KOH, the specific capacitance of 
GCK-3 is the largest, and the specific capacitance of the current density 
at 1 A g
� 1 
is 234 F g
� 1
. To explore its practicability, an SSC based on 
GCK-3 was assembled. The test results show that SSC can work stably in 
the voltage range of 0 – 1.4 V, and the energy density is 13.7 Wh kg
� 1 
when the power density is 350 W kg
� 1
. This study provides a good 
reference value for the efficient utilization of natural biomass waste and 
the preparation of high-performance energy storage conversion 
materials.
